messages.subject: Queueing theory distributions
parts:
I'm trying to relate service level to load in a queueing theory setting, and I don't see a built-in sampling distribution that fits that today.

If, for example, I have a queueing system with m servers and with a utilization of rho (ratio of offered load and capacity), then queueing::C_erlang() returns the probability that an incoming service request will need to wait in queue.  By the latter part of https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2001-September/014986.html and the code for C_erlang, I can express that in R.  With a bit further manipulation, I can get service level--the probability that an incoming service request will have to wait longer than t seconds to be served.

If I did that right (I seem to get the same answers using the queueing package and this), the R code looks like

      erlb <- function(nsrv, nerl, log=FALSE)
      {
        # Returns Erlang-B blockage for nsrv servers and nerl erlangs of traffic.
        # If log=TRUE, then logarithm of the blockage is returned.  Works for all
        # nsrv>=0 and all nerl>=0.  Both nsrv and nerl can be non-integers.

        # Same as queueing::B_erlang
        # From https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2001-September/014986.html
        # See, too, https://ia601606.us.archive.org/26/items/bstj53-3-525/bstj53-3-525_text.pdf

        lnerlb<-
          dgamma(nerl, shape=nsrv+1, scale=1, log=TRUE) -
          pgamma(nerl, shape=nsrv+1, scale=1, log.p=TRUE, lower.tail=FALSE) ;
          if (log) lnerlb else exp(lnerlb)
      }

      erlc <- function (c = 1, r = 0)
      {
          # Same as queueing::C_erlang but with erlb instead of B_erlang
          ## if (is.anomalous(c))
          ##     stop("The parameter c is anomalous. Check it!")
          ## if (is.anomalous(r))
          ##     stop("The parameter r is anomalous. Check it!")
          ## if (c < 1)
          ##     stop(ALL_c_warning)
          ## if (!is.wholenumber(c))
          ##     stop(ALL_c_integer)
          b_result <- erlb(c - 1, r)
          (r * b_result)/(c - (r * (1 - b_result)))
      }

      SLfun <- function(rho, M, ts, t) {
        # M = number of servers
        # rho = utilization (fraction of available time servers are busy)
        # ts = expected value of service time in seconds
        # t = SL time in seconds
          SL  <- (erlc(M, rho * M) *
                  exp(-M * (1 - rho) * t / ts))
          1 - SL
      }



Because I don't know capacity well, I'd like to do a Stan model that looks something like

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                      // no. of days of data
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] sl;       // daily recorded service level
  int<lower=1> M;                      // no. of servers
  vector<lower=0>[N] load;             // load in units of time
  vector<lower=0>[N] recordedcapacity; // capacity in the same units of time
  real<lower=1> t;                     // Time threshold for calculating SL
  real<lower=1> ts;                    // average service time
}

transformed data {
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] recordedrho;
  recordedrho <- load / recordedcapacity;
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  vector<lower=0>[N] capacity;
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] rho;
  rho <- load / capacity;
}

model {
  rho ~ normal(recordedrho, sigma) T[0.0, 1.0];  // there's probably a better distribution for this
  sl ~ SLfun(rho, M, ts, t);
}


It's probably simple algebra, but I'm missing how to convert SLfun into Stan functions, presumably built into a functions {} block with Stan's gamma distribution functions.  Pointers?

Bill

The place to look is the manual --- there's a chapter on
user-defined functions that shows you how to write a new
density and there's a reference chapter on all the densities.
Assuming you want to do this all on the log scale, it'd
look something like:

functions {
real erlb(...) {

}
real erlc(...) {
...
}
real SL_log(real rho, int M, real ts, real t) {
return log1m(erlc(M, rho * M) * exp(-M * (1 - rho) * t / ts));
}
}

I removed the "fun" suffix and added the required "_log" for densities
and returned on the log scale. And I just chose the log scale --- it's
all you need for Stan, so I wouldn't add all the flags you have in the R
code.

Then you just need to define the other functions pretty much the same
way as in R.

- Bob

qplot(c(1,1000), stat='function', fun=function (x) {B_erlang(c=20, u = x)}, geom='line')

I created Stan wrappers for some of the gamma distributions in Stan (existing names prepended with "S"), and I thought something like this might work:

qplot(c(1,1000), stat='function', fun=function (x) {exp(Sgamma_log(x, alpha=21, beta = 1)-Sgamma_cdf_log(x,alpha=21,beta=1))}, geom='line')

but it doesn't work.  Even getting away from the failed plot,

x<-10;Sgamma_log(x, 21, 1)-Sgamma_cdf_log(x,21,1)

doesn't produce the same answers.  So I'm either missing the correspondence between functions or the parameterization of the functions.

Bill

Yes, if it's a distribution it should return a real. That's
what's going to get added to the log density and it should
be the sum of all the log densities of the vectorized components.
